goals: Recognise when the target is a count
Fit a Poisson regression and interpret coefficients as rate ratios
why: Insurance claim counts, website visits, defects and footfall are counts. OLS can predict negative counts and gets the variance wrong; Poisson regression handles both.
explain: Counts are whole numbers ≥ 0 and their variance usually grows with the mean. A **Poisson regression** models the **log of the expected count** as a linear function of the features.
Because of the log, coefficients are **multiplicative**: e^b is a **rate ratio**. b = 0.2 → e^0.2 ≈ 1.22 → a 22% higher expected count per unit increase.

It belongs to the **GLM** (generalised linear model) family: pick a distribution (normal, binomial, Poisson, gamma) and a link function (identity, logit, log). Logistic regression is the binomial GLM.
If the variance is much larger than the mean (**over-dispersion**), use negative binomial regression. Use an **exposure/offset** when the observation windows differ (claims per policy-year).

formula.tex: P(Y = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}, \qquad \log \mu = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + \dots + b_p x_p
formula.plain: Left: the chance of exactly k events when the average rate is λ. Right: Poisson regression makes the log of the expected count μ a weighted sum of the features.

example.title: Staffing a toll booth
steps: Weekday afternoons: cars arrive at an average of λ = 3 per minute; one lane can process 5 per minute
example.result: About 8% of minutes overload the lane. A Poisson regression of arrivals on hour, day and weather gives λ for every hour of the week, so the operator can staff lanes accordingly.

practice.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
young = rng.integers(0, 2, 2000); km = rng.uniform(0.5, 3, 2000)
claims = rng.poisson(np.exp(-2.3 + 0.4 * young + 0.1 * km))
m = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0).fit(np.c_[young, km], claims)
print(np.exp(m.coef_).round(2))      # rate ratios ≈ [1.49, 1.11]

check.q: Poisson coefficient b = 0.7. The rate ratio is about…
check.why: e^0.7 ≈ 2.01, so the count roughly doubles.
